Report: Samsung Heads All-In on 7th-Generation DRAM, Establishes Mass-Production TF Within Memory Division

According to Korean media reports, Samsung Electronics’ Semiconductor (DS) Division’s Memory Business Unit has formed a new task force (TF) responsible for the final Process Architecture (PA) stage of pilot production for its 10 nm 7th-generation DRAM (D1d), and is bolstering internal staffing accordingly. The Semiconductor Research Institute already houses a DRAM Technology Development (TD) organization, and a dedicated D1d development team is in operation.

This TF is interpreted as Samsung’s all-out effort to maximize product maturity.

Through this TF, Samsung aims to accelerate next-generation DRAM mass production. High-density, high-performance DRAM is essential for mass-producing 6th-generation HBM4—a potential game-changer in the HBM market. D1d demands finer technical capabilities than D1c, which some competitors have claimed to have successfully developed. The 10 nm-class DRAM process has progressed through 1x (1st gen), 1y (2nd gen), 1z (3rd gen), 1a (4th gen), 1b (5th gen), and 1c (6th gen). Each successive node narrows circuit linewidths, boosting performance and energy efficiency. D1d follows directly after D1c.

Samsung’s Semiconductor Research Institute also operates an “ultra-fine DRAM process–dedicated TF” targeting sub-10 nm single-digit precision, demonstrating the company’s determination to reclaim its “ultra-lead” edge.

An industry insider commented, “Amid fears of falling behind peers, Samsung is determined not to falter on next-generation products. Securing yields is critical for advanced nodes, so they are pooling talent to mass-produce highly refined chips.”

Samsung’s TF initiative is part of a broader strategy to reverse its recent underperformance relative to competitors. Although Samsung was first in the world to develop 5th-generation DRAM (D1b) at the end of 2022 and began mass production in May 2023, it failed to secure adequate yields, delaying follow-on products and eroding competitiveness.

By contrast, SK Hynix and Micron—initially one step behind Samsung on 5th-generation DRAM—both succeeded in commercializing D1b within the same year. SK Hynix completed 6th-generation DRAM (D1c) development last year and reportedly conducted a Process Reliability Assessment (PRA) for D1d in August. Given that a first PRA typically follows immediately after design, observers believe SK Hynix’s D1d development may be somewhat ahead of Samsung’s. Micron also shipped samples of DDR5 based on its “1γ” process (equivalent to D1c) to potential customers last month.

Samsung, meanwhile, continues to struggle. Industry analysts attribute this to lingering employee dissatisfaction over years of personnel treatment, repeated internal transfers, and departures to rivals—resulting in the loss of experienced mentors and ultimately yield challenges. Reports suggest the yield on Samsung’s in-development 6th-generation DRAM remains in the single digits. Another insider noted, “Closed organizational culture and hard-to-measure MBO targets inhibit focus on development and analysis. Shortening communication cycles is also necessary.”

The decision to deploy a 7th-generation DRAM mass-production TF is seen as a bold play to overcome these hurdles. Some view the TF’s formation as a “positive signal” that Samsung has reached sufficient technical maturity in D1d to enter the PA stage. Historically, Samsung has advanced to PA only after achieving a certain level of R&D completion on next-generation DRAM.

However, pursuing both 6th- and 7th-generation DRAM development concurrently is viewed as a drawback. Having completed 6th-generation DRAM last year, SK Hynix can now concentrate fully on the 7th generation, whereas Samsung must allocate resources across both nodes.

SK Hynix has already secured manufacturability for 6th-generation DRAM and plans to integrate it into mainstream products in H2 2025. It has stated that this year’s investments will focus on high-bandwidth memory (HBM) and infrastructure. At its January earnings briefing, SK Hynix announced plans to apply its 1c process to HBM4E, aligning development and supply to maintain market leadership.

The industry is closely watching whether Samsung, having trailed SK Hynix on 6th-generation DRAM, can turn the tide through successful 7th-generation DRAM development. No company has yet achieved mass production of 7th-generation DRAM. Samsung plans to commence mass production of its 10 nm-class D1d in 2026 and its sub-10 nm 1st-generation DRAM (D0a) in 2027.

Report: SK Hynix to end DDR4 production by 2Q26

The two major South Korean DRAM manufacturers are each preparing to discontinue their older DDR4 production lines. Following Samsung Electronics' early April announcement of its end-of-life (EOL) plan, SK Hynix recently notified suppliers with an EOL letter regarding DDR4 chips. The company plans to phase out 8GB and 16GB DDR4 chips produced using the 1z nanometer process, officially entering the discontinuation stage by April 2026.

According to SK Hynix's notification, DDR4 chips based on the 1z nanometer process for PC and server applications—specifically 8GB and 16GB products including epitaxy wafers, components, and SO-DIMM modules—will also be discontinued. The last order date is set for October 2025, with final shipments expected in April 2026. SK Hynix declined to comment on this matter.

Market shifts and price impact
With the EOL announcements from these South Korean DRAM giants taking effect, DDR4 market prices have risen significantly. Industry observers believe that SK Hynix's decision to cease production of the 1z nanometer process, which belongs to older lines not utilizing EUV equipment, reflects a "natural reduction" in output caused by transitioning to advanced manufacturing processes. This strategy aims to stop supplying from outdated production lines.

Upgrading existing equipment and shifting to newer manufacturing processes will substantially reduce mature-process DRAM output across the industry.

Since the third quarter of 2024, original manufacturers have been cutting back consumer DDR4 supplies to prevent rapid price declines. Industry sources indicate that due to reduced supply from major players, DRAM shortages could emerge as early as summer 2025.

Recently, SK Hynix's DRAM chip prices have increased by more than 10%. Taiwanese suppliers face challenges securing stable DDR4 sources because DDR4 still holds a significant market share in consumer and industrial control sectors. Ensuring a steady supply from both major vendors will be difficult, likely causing volatile pricing in the short term.

Micron's stance and Taiwan's opportunity
Earlier reports speculated that Micron might join the DDR4 production cuts, but the company remains tight-lipped about any discontinuation plans.

A Taiwanese memory module manufacturer noted that although Chinese producers have greatly expanded DDR4 capacity, customers remain cautious about exporting overseas or serving specific industrial markets. Currently, the three leading DRAM makers rely mainly on Micron as a key supplier, while Taiwan's Nanya is expected to benefit most from redirected orders.

According to manufacturing sources, Nanya's DDR4 capacity is limited. Many downstream companies have sought supplies from Nanya recently, but short-term volumes cannot meet demand. Winbond has actively shifted toward DDR4 production since early 2025 and may also join the order transfer trend as it upgrades processes and expands production scale.

Inventory dynamics and demand revival
Following recent announcements from original manufacturers ceasing DDR4 product supply, spot market availability of DDR4 chips has tightened. On the demand side, PC manufacturers have consumed inventory over several quarters, showing clear stock depletion effects. Mobile clients, who previously maintained healthy inventories, have begun replenishing stocks, driving up prices for DDR4 and LPDDR4X accordingly.

Amid the accelerated restructuring of the DRAM industry driven by high-bandwidth memory (HBM), the global DRAM ecosystem faces critical transformation. According to statistics, the worldwide DRAM market size reached US$26.729 billion in the first quarter of 2025, representing a 42.5% year-over-year increase.

HBM: The future growth engine
SK Hynix leveraged its absolute advantage in the HBM sector to dethrone Samsung after more than 40 years as market leader, capturing a 36.7% market share for the first time and claiming the top position. Samsung's share dropped to 35.6%.

Data from China's CFM indicates that the gap between SK Hynix and Samsung in DRAM narrowed in 2024, especially impacted by AI chip export controls and delayed demand for HBM3E 12-layer products. These factors hurt Samsung's HBM sales in the first quarter of 2025, resulting in a 17% quarter-over-quarter revenue decline and loss of its DRAM leadership.

The organization forecasts that HBM market penetration will double from 9% in 2023 to 18% in 2024, with expectations to surpass 30% in 2025. This growth positions HBM as the core driver of the DRAM industry, prompting major manufacturers to intensify technology competition and accelerate the phasing out of old process line supplies.

Report: Samsung Raises DRAM Prices… A Rare 'Spring' for Memory

According to South Korean media reports, Samsung Electronics finalized plans to increase DRAM supply prices with major customers earlier this month. While the specifics vary by customer, the average price hike is reportedly in the double-digit range for DDR4 DRAM and single-digit range for DDR5 DRAM. DDR4 prices are said to have increased by 20%, while DDR5 rose by around 5%.

An industry official familiar with the matter stated, “Samsung Electronics has signed DRAM supply contracts with customers at increased prices,” adding, “DRAM prices are rising across the semiconductor industry.”

This is the first time Samsung has raised DRAM prices this year and the first such move in nearly a year.

Last year, DRAM faced declining demand and oversupply. According to market research firm DRAMeXchange, the average fixed transaction price for PC DRAM standard products (DDR4 8Gb 1Gx8) fell by 20.59% in November alone after entering a downtrend in the second half. This trend continued with a flat performance through the first quarter of this year.

Signs of change emerged in April. Micron, the third-largest DRAM supplier based in the U.S., pushed for price hikes. While Micron cited increased tariffs by the Trump administration, the move is interpreted as being driven by strong demand.

Indeed, DRAM fixed transaction prices began rising in April. Last month, the price of PC DDR4 8Gb (1Gx8 2133MHz) increased by 22.22% from the previous month. This marked the first fixed price hike since April of last year.

As the world’s largest memory supplier, Samsung tends to be cautious about price adjustments, indicating that demand must have been particularly strong.

It is believed that a surge in inventory buildup demand played a major role. Orders from PC, mobile, and server manufacturers increased as they sought to stock up on DRAM before the burden of Trump-era tariffs intensified.

At Samsung’s Q1 earnings call held on April 30, Memory Business Division Executive Vice President Kim Jae-joon stated, “Due to concerns over global tariff changes, prebuild (early inventory buildup) of complete sets has expanded, and customer component inventories have been depleted faster than expected.”

Another factor believed to have driven demand is the perception that DRAM prices are currently at their lowest point.

With rising demand and prices, the memory industry is expected to enjoy a rare tailwind. Until now, high-bandwidth memory (HBM) driven by AI demand had been the standout performer, but a recovery in general-purpose DRAM demand is now becoming visible.

The DRAM prices negotiated with individual customers are expected to remain in effect for several months, enabling the companies to maintain profitability for a while. This price increase will be reflected in Q2 earnings and is expected to contribute to improved profitability.

The semiconductor industry is now watching closely to see whether this DRAM upturn will continue.

Semiconductor Equipment / Foundry: Marginal Improvement in Industry Sentiment
 JP Morgan (J. Kwon, May 20, 2025)

1QCY25 results and outlook indicate that as chip stacking and process node evolution continues, demand for testing high-performance memory such as HBM (High Bandwidth Memory) and DDR5 is rising sharply. This is driving stable to mid-single-digit growth in both front-end and back-end testing and wafer fabrication equipment (WFE) markets. While the WFE market is projected to reach approximately $100 billion for the full year 2025 with a broadly optimistic outlook for 2026, macroeconomic and geopolitical uncertainties—especially tariffs—in 2H25 remain key concerns. We prefer Samsung Electronics (SEC), SK Hynix, Tokyo Electron, Advantest, and Hanmi to capture long-term structural opportunities.

• WFE Market: Solid Growth Momentum

• Leading manufacturers forecast the 2025 WFE market at $99–110 billion, indicating stable to mid-single-digit growth.

• Leading equipment vendors (LAM, KLA) are optimistic about continued adoption by leading foundries and logic fabs. Tokyo Electron expects double-digit growth in 2026.

• DRAM and NAND together are projected to account for around 35% of WFE demand, with DRAM growing to 20% due to HBM and DDR5 transitions, and NAND reaching 10%.

My thoughts on @dMatrix_AI and 3D-stacked digital in-memory compute (3DIMC):

d-Matrix is taking direct aim at the memory wall with 3DIMC, vertically stacking DRAM with logic dies (see image below). The company claims a 10x boost in bandwidth and 10x better energy efficiency versus HBM4. These gains could reshape inference economics in an era where datacenter power is capped and agentic AI demands low-latency interactivity and high throughput at scale.

There’s precedent here. Nearly 20 years ago, AMD bet on stacked DRAM and co-developed HBM. The early pain of costly interposers and low yields gave the industry a blueprint for high-bandwidth memory that still underpins today’s AI accelerators. But even with HBM, compute has scaled far faster than memory throughput, and accelerators increasingly sit idle waiting for data.

If d-Matrix can deliver on 3DIMC, it could play a similar role for the inference era that HBM did for the GPU era. But this is an early announcement, so we need to see measured performance on actual silicon in customers' hands. The company says it's working with some of the world’s largest hyperscalers and neoclouds; will these customers put 3DIMC into production?

- 3D DRAM vs HBM: cost, yield, and IP model of 3D DRAM — proprietary to d-Matrix or licensed?

Long-term: could this architecture ever extend beyond datacenter into edge devices, or will costs or thermal/mechanical concerns keep it confined to servers?

$NVDA $AMD Channel checks across more than 50 industry contacts indicate that underlying demand for accelerator GPUs remains exceptionally robust, with reported unit or dollar growth of 10‑50 % year‑over‑year driven almost entirely by generative‑AI inference roll‑outs and the continued build‑out of training clusters. Lead times for high‑end NVIDIA parts are still quoted at 9‑18 months and, despite isolated anecdotes of improved availability, most hyperscalers and enterprise VARs describe persistent allocation, especially on networking cards and HBM‑attached SKUs. The structural driver remains the widening gap between conventional CPU performance and the compute and memory‑bandwidth requirements of large language models, which is forcing virtually every new AI workload to deploy on a GPU or an ASIC that copies the NVIDIA programming model.

Pricing dynamics are bifurcating sharply. Street‑level quotes for the current‑generation H100 have started to compress by 5‑20 % as AMD’s MI300A/X family enters volume and some channel partners seek to clear inventory ahead of Blackwell. By contrast, forward contracts for Blackwell GB200 blades, particularly the NVL72 racks, are closing at a meaningful premium to H100—often list or better—because hyperscalers value the node‑count reduction and energy savings the new architecture delivers. Enterprises without deep AI engineering talent are willing to trade price for access to performance per watt, leading to a two‑tier market in which trailing silicon commoditises quickly while bleeding‑edge SKUs remain supply‑constrained and margin‑rich. Importantly, several contacts highlighted intensifying price sensitivity in cloud GPU rentals; that is likely to force public cloud providers either to accept lower margins or to migrate more rapidly toward internally designed accelerators.

On the supply side, the real bottleneck is shifting from GPU die output to the memory and power infrastructure that surrounds the silicon. HBM3E capacity at both Samsung and Micron is effectively sold out through at least calendar Q4 and the incremental expansion of TSV lines is gating volume for every vendor, including AMD. Power‑delivery constraints inside new data‑centre builds are also starting to cap near‑term rack deployments; multiple cloud architects cite substation delays of up to 18 months as the critical path rather than board availability. That dynamic favours vertically integrated players such as Microsoft and Alphabet that can secure incremental megawatts and reinforces the scarcity value of any chip that can deliver higher performance per watt—again underscoring why Blackwell and MI300X pricing is proving so resilient.

Performance interviews show that memory‑bandwidth, not raw FLOPs, is now the dominant purchase criterion. AMD is leveraging its Infinity Architecture and superior HBM bandwidth to win inference‑heavy workloads where latency matters more than absolute training throughput, while NVIDIA retains a decisive advantage in scaled training jobs thanks to its mature software stack and NVLink‑enabled cluster architecture. The widening focus on energy efficiency per token trained is stimulating interest in custom silicon, but timelines for most first‑party ASICs remain 2026+. Consequently, the established GPU incumbents should enjoy at least 6‑8 more quarters of outsized gross‑profit capture before meaningful disintermediation risk appears.

Competitive share trends reveal that AMD has pushed to roughly 40 % of data‑centre CPU shipments and is closing the gap in AI accelerators faster than expected, primarily by pricing aggressively and exploiting NVIDIA’s allocation constraints. Intel’s Gaudi roadmap is failing to resonate; its server CPU share has collapsed from 95 % to roughly 55 % over the last half‑decade and our contacts see no catalyst for reversal. Despite headline share erosion, NVIDIA still commands 90‑92 % of installed AI training capacity and, given two successive architecture wins (Hopper then Blackwell), is positioned to hold the lion’s share of training workloads through at least 2025. In networking, Broadcom’s dominance in switch ASICs persists, but early demand for NVIDIA’s Spectrum‑X Ethernet portfolio is emerging as the first credible threat in years; Marvell is seeing traction mainly where hyperscalers want custom silicon over merchant parts.

Investment implications are multifaceted. For NVIDIA, the data confirm that unit demand and mix are both skewing to higher‑ASP, higher‑margin products, providing clear earnings‑per‑share upside versus current sell‑side models that already assume mid‑teens sequential revenue growth into FY26; the key risk is whether power and HBM constraints cap shipment volumes below order books. For AMD, each percentage‑point of incremental accelerator share could translate to roughly USD 600‑800 M of annualised revenue given prevailing ASPs; however, sustainability depends on its ability to move to an annual cadence and secure enough HBM, which remains uncertain. Intel remains structurally challenged; without a competitive accelerator and with Sapphire Rapids yields still lagging, the company faces further gross‑margin compression and share loss, suggesting any long thesis must hinge on foundry optionality rather than product strength. Memory vendors Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron are positioned for outsized pricing power and margin expansion as HBM3E drags up blended DRAM ASPs; Micron, with the smallest installed DRAM base but fastest HBM ramp, offers the highest operating‑leverage torque. Broadcom’s switch ASIC franchise should continue compounding at mid‑teens with limited risk in the next 4‑6 quarters, but investors must monitor NVIDIA’s Ethernet attach as a potential headwind to 2026 growth. Finally, data‑centre REITs and power‑infrastructure suppliers may become critical ancillary beneficiaries, yet the long lead‑time nature of substation capacity injects a timing mismatch that could temper near‑term capital returns.

From a portfolio‑construction perspective, the read‑through argues for maintaining an overweight NVIDIA core position while opportunistically adding AMD on supply‑related pullbacks, pairing both against an underweight Intel. Layering in a long Micron or SK Hynix position hedges against any GPU unit volatility, as HBM scarcity should support memory margins even in a slower server upgrade cycle. Alpha generation will likely pivot on monitoring two variables: the pace at which Blackwell ramps relative to MI300X and any sign that hyperscale budgets rotate from GPUs toward internally developed ASICs sooner than 2026.

$MU $NVDA $TSM $VRT Micron’s guidance revision is unambiguously constructive for the generative AI infrastructure cycle and, importantly, it is pricing-led. For FQ4’25 (quarter ending 8/28/25), Micron raised revenue to $11.2B ±$0.1B from $10.7B ±$0.3B, lifted non‑GAAP gross margin to 44.5% ±0.5% from 42.0% ±1.0%, and took non‑GAAP EPS to $2.85 ±$0.07 from $2.50 ±$0.15, while tightening ranges. The midpoint raises imply +$0.5B revenue (+4.7%) and +2.5 ppts of gross margin vs prior guidance, with non‑GAAP opex nudged to $1.22B ±$0.015B from $1.20B ±$0.02B. Management explicitly attributes the revision to better pricing, particularly in DRAM, and strong execution. In other words, this is not a “one‑customer pull‑in” story; it reads as broad memory pricing strength in the quarter. (Micron Technology, Reuters)

Context strengthens the signal. Micron entered the quarter with HBM effectively sold out for CY25 and with HBM pricing largely pre‑determined, so an in‑quarter beat from “improved DRAM pricing” most likely reflects firmer conventional DRAM (server DDR5, mobile LPDDR5X, graphics GDDR) layered on top of locked‑in HBM volume. That is consistent with Micron’s June commentary that HBM revenue was inflecting and with 3rd‑party models that peg FY25 HBM revenue around $6B. The through‑line is that the AI compute buildout remains robust enough to tighten memory markets beyond HBM. (Micron Technology, Morningstar)

Demand drivers remain extraordinary and increasingly memory‑intensive. Hyperscaler capex is still stepping up: Microsoft has repeatedly telegraphed ~$80B of FY25 AI data center investment, Alphabet raised 2025 capex to roughly $85B, and Meta narrowed 2025 capex to $66–72B, explicitly citing GenAI scaling. On the deployment side, NVIDIA’s Blackwell platforms structurally raise memory content per accelerator: a DGX B200 node advertises 1.44 TB of HBM across 8 GPUs, and an NVL72 rack domain lists up to 13.4 TB of HBM3E; Blackwell Ultra B300 pushes to 288 GB HBM3E per GPU. Rising HBM per GPU, plus larger NVLink domains, translate directly into more bits per rack and higher memory dollar content per rack—even before you consider conventional DRAM on host CPUs. This is exactly the kind of mix shift that supports Micron’s pricing‑led upside. (The Official Microsoft Blog, Seeking Alpha, Meta, NVIDIA, Tom's Hardware)

Supply remains the swing factor, and the latest data points cut in favor of continued tightness through 2H25. TSMC’s CoWoS advanced‑packaging capacity, a known bottleneck for GPU+HBM systems, is expanding materially in 2025 toward ~60–75k wafers/month, which helps system availability but also enables HBM attachment to scale without flooding supply. Meanwhile, competitive dynamics in HBM continue to concentrate near‑term share at SK hynix and Micron; reports of Samsung’s slower 12‑Hi HBM3E qualification have persisted into mid‑2025, even as Samsung works to catch up. SK hynix, for its part, now frames AI memory TAM growth at ~30% CAGR to 2030, reinforcing a multi‑year runway for HBM and adjacent memory. The net is that 2H25 capacity relief is real at the packaging layer, but HBM stacking and validation remain the scarcer assets—supportive of price/mix and of Micron’s updated guide. (DIGITIMES Asia, TrendForce, Reuters)

Near‑term price action corroborates the thesis. Independent trackers flag sharp 3Q25 price increases for several DRAM categories as suppliers reallocate legacy capacity toward server and HBM. TrendForce has flagged double‑digit sequential moves in DDR4 and graphics DRAM and a 15–20% lift in HBM pricing into 3Q25. NAND is firming but less acute, with enterprise SSD contract pricing modeled up ~5–10% in 3Q25. Micron’s guidance revision lands squarely in this environment of tightening memory supply and rising DRAM ASPs. (Tom's Hardware, TrendForce)

For the broader generative AI infrastructure ecosystem, there are 6 investable implications. First, the profit pool is shifting incrementally toward memory through at least the Blackwell ramp. GPU BOMs are increasingly memory‑heavy and, while NVIDIA retains substantial pricing power, higher HBM and DRAM costs either compress accelerator margins or pass through into higher system ASPs. Given sustained demand elasticity in training capacity, we do not expect meaningful order deferrals; however, we do expect a rising memory share of rack‑level spend in 2H25–1H26, which accrues to HBM suppliers and to those with advantaged power/performance (e.g., Micron’s 12‑Hi 36 GB HBM3E). (Micron Technology)

Second, this update reduces the probability that memory availability will be the gating factor for Blackwell deployments in 4Q25–1H26; packaging and power look like the tighter constraints. NVIDIA itself underscores the power density of NVL72‑class racks, and supply chain checks continue to emphasize liquid cooling and power delivery as critical path items. That tilts incremental alpha toward data center power and thermal names with validated NVL72/GB300 reference designs, as well as optical interconnect suppliers riding the 800G→1.6T transition. (TrendForce, PR Newswire, Cignal AI)

Third, advanced packaging scarcity is easing but still strategic. As CoWoS output rises, substrate and interposer ecosystems remain tight but investable. TSMC’s step‑up through 2025 supports GPU+HBM shipments and should translate into continued backlog burn for substrate houses and organic RDL suppliers tied to CoWoS‑L and NVLink domains. We would fade the idea that packaging bottlenecks will structurally cap 2025 volumes; the bigger swing now is how quickly HBM 12‑Hi yields normalize at each DRAM vendor. (TrendForce)

Fourth, optics/networking remains a secular beneficiary rather than a budget casualty. Even with memory inflation, total AI rack budgets are expanding, not contracting, and 800G shipments are re‑accelerating with early 1.6T programs entering select deployments tied to Blackwell. The mix shift to larger NVLink or Ethernet memory‑coherent domains sustains switch ASIC, optical module, and NIC growth. We maintain an overweight stance on suppliers levered to 800G and early 1.6T ramps. (Cignal AI, https://t.co/wctbcPCigO)

Fifth, storage tightness is emerging but is secondary to DRAM. Enterprise SSD pricing is trending up mid‑single to low‑double digits into 3Q25, a modest headwind to AI factory TCO but not enough to alter deployment trajectories. The bigger architecture shift to watch is the industry’s exploration of tiered memory, including “high‑bandwidth flash” concepts that could augment HBM with stacked NAND for inference at lower cost/bit; these are longer‑dated (earliest 2027) and do not change 2025–2026 dynamics. (TrendForce, Tom's Hardware)

Sixth, policy is a 2026 risk rather than a 2025 blocker. The latest tariff rhetoric—100% chip tariffs on some imports with exemptions for companies manufacturing in the U.S., and separate arrangements with South Korea mitigating disadvantages—adds uncertainty to 2026 supply chains and pricing but has not derailed current AI memory flows. We treat it as volatility fuel rather than base‑case disruption for 2H25. (Reuters)

Investment implications are clear. For memory, the guidance lift validates a pricing and mix tailwind into the Blackwell ramp. We would add on weakness to high‑quality HBM‑levered names with proven 12‑Hi roadmaps and sold‑out 2025 books. In Micron’s case, the combination of a ~$0.5B revenue uplift, +2.5 ppts gross margin, and +14% EPS raise on pricing strength argues for upward estimate revisions into FY26 and supports the view that memory suppliers will take a larger slice of AI economics near term. The primary risk is 2026 HBM price normalization if TSV capacity and 12‑Hi yields overshoot demand; several watchers already flag double‑digit HBM price decline risk next year. We would manage this by trimming exposure as order books fill and by rotating into NAND‑heavy franchises or diversified memory names with 1‑gamma cost downs that can defend margins in a down‑ASP tape. (TrendForce)

For accelerators, the takeaway is slightly mixed but net positive. Strong memory pricing points to a healthy GPU pipeline, and CoWoS expansions reduce the chance that packaging caps shipments; however, BOM inflation from HBM can pressure accelerator margins at the margin if list prices are held flat into large pre‑negotiated CSP contracts. Given demand intensity, we still expect pass‑through to hold, but we would watch for scattered signs of CSPs optimizing configs (e.g., deferring 12‑Hi adoption in some inference footprints or mixing HBM capacities across racks) if HBM pricing stays at the top of the guided range. (TrendForce)

For data center power, cooling, and optics, the signal remains “go.” If memory is not the gating factor for 4Q25, the bottlenecks revert to power availability, liquid cooling, optics, and integration, all of which still show order strength. Names with validated NVL72/GB300 reference designs, liquid cooling IP, and 800G/1.6T exposure should continue to print above‑trend orders; the guidance shift from Micron reduces the tail risk of AI rack pushouts due to memory shortages. (https://t.co/2HXajdJv8P, Cignal AI)

Bottom line for the IC: Micron’s pricing‑driven guide raise is a high‑quality confirmation that AI memory remains the tightest, most value‑accretive component of the AI rack in 2H25. We would keep memory and advanced‑packaging beneficiaries as core longs through the Blackwell ramp, pair them against more consumer‑exposed DRAM names vulnerable to DDR4 price spikes, and lean into power/cooling and 800G optics as the next‑order constraints that convert directly into revenue. We would also start pre‑positioning for 2026 HBM price normalization risk by favoring suppliers with clear HBM4 transition plans, cost‑down nodes (1‑gamma), and balanced mix across DRAM and NAND so that gross margin resilience survives the inevitable ASP giveback. $NVDA $AMD $AVGO $INTC The roadmap shows that the performance race in data‑center AI silicon is now primarily a packaging and memory race. Across 2025‑2028, the center of gravity shifts from monolithic silicon interposers (CoWoS‑S) to RDL‑based organic interposers with embedded silicon bridges (CoWoS‑L) for the highest‑end parts, while cost‑optimized designs adopt RDL interposers without large silicon (CoWoS‑R). That shift is driven by the need to exceed 3.3× reticle‑size packages, add more HBM stacks, and reduce the yield risk and cost of massive interposers. TSMC’s own technical disclosures set the guardrails: CoWoS‑S supports up to 3.3× reticle (~2,700 mm²) with deep trench capacitors (eDTC) in silicon, CoWoS‑R delivers 2/2 µm RDL on organic interposers, and CoWoS‑L combines wide‑pitch RDL with embedded Local Silicon Interconnect (LSI) that restores sub‑micron routing density and allows embedded eDTC under logic dies; TSMC began CoWoS‑L volume in 2024. For workloads that want even more HBM, TSMC has publicly discussed moving from 3.3× to 5.5× reticle packages with up to 12 HBM stacks in 2025‑2026 and targeting 9× reticle by 2027. The net implication is clear: package size, interconnect density, and power delivery—not just transistor count—are the limiting factors for next‑gen AI systems. (https://t.co/oi9tKsdRLQ, TSMC, TrendForce)

Reading the roadmap by brand, the pattern is consistent with those technical constraints. NVIDIA’s H200 stays on CoWoS‑S with 141 GB of HBM3E, while Blackwell B200/GB200 move to CoWoS‑L with 192 GB of HBM3E, reflecting a package architecture change aimed at larger die complexes and more memory per GPU. AMD’s MI325X shipped with 256 GB, and the MI350 series is positioned at 288 GB HBM3E; both are CoWoS‑S today, with MI350 on newer process nodes and Micron publicly confirmed as a 12‑high HBM3E supplier to that platform. Intel’s Gaudi 3, fabbed on TSMC N5, uses 128 GB of HBM2E and remains on CoWoS‑S. Google’s Trillium/TPU v6e doubles HBM capacity and bandwidth versus v5e, also consistent with CoWoS‑class integration. Microsoft’s Maia 100 uses CoWoS‑S with 64 GB of HBM2E, explicitly trading to a less supply‑constrained HBM generation. Amazon’s Trainium2 advertises 96 GB HBM3E; credible industry reporting and disclosures describe a dual‑chiplet die with 4 HBM stacks on CoWoS‑S/R, which matches the “CoWoS‑R” callout in the chart. Meta’s MTIA 2 targets inference and uses 128 GB of LPDDR5 instead of HBM, a deliberate cost/power choice. These public facts substantiate the broad directions in the chart while reminding us that some rows (e.g., far‑future NVIDIA “VR”/“Feynman” and several 2027‑2028 entries) are directional rather than confirmed. (NVIDIA, Wccftech, AMD, Micron Technology, Intel CDRD, Google Cloud, ServeTheHome, Amazon Web Services, Inc., Meta AI)

Two supply bottlenecks dominate the investable landscape: CoWoS capacity and HBM supply. TSMC’s CoWoS output roughly doubled in 2024 and is on track to expand again in 2025; multiple industry trackers see 2025 monthly capacity in the 65k‑75k wafers range with further growth into 2026, yet demand still exceeds supply and pricing for CoWoS has risen by 10‑20%. On the memory side, SK hynix has had the volume and technical lead in HBM3/HBM3E, Micron is rapidly gaining share with 12‑high HBM3E and targets 20‑25% share, and Samsung is working to re‑establish leadership as HBM4 approaches. The price environment remains firm: several trackers have called out rising DRAM/HBM pricing into 2025, and HBM’s share of DRAM value is climbing into double digits. GPU sellers cannot ship without both CoWoS capacity and qualified HBM, which keeps the supply chain tight and shifts value capture upstream. (TrendForce, Micron Technology, Barron's)

How CoWoS‑S is built. CoWoS stands for chip‑on‑wafer‑on‑substrate. In CoWoS‑S, TSMC fabricates a passive silicon interposer (often on mature nodes like 65/55 nm) with TSVs and fine‑pitch BEOL routing, and integrates deep trench capacitors into the interposer to stiffen the power‑delivery network. Known‑good logic dies and HBM stacks are flip‑chip attached to the interposer at wafer scale, underfilled, and molded; after wafer‑level assembly the system is diced and mounted to an ABF organic substrate for board‑level attach and test. Critical materials and tools include copper plating and RDL patterning (Applied Materials Raider/Nokota, Lam’s SABRE and wet cleans), photosensitive polyimides and PBO dielectrics for RDL (HD Microsystems and peers), capillary and molded underfills (Namics; MR‑MUF is a well‑documented HBM process advantage at SK hynix), and temporary bonding/debonding and wafer handling systems for 2.5D/3D stacks (EV Group). Substrates use Ajinomoto Build‑up Film dielectric and are supplied by Ibiden, Shinko, Unimicron, AT&S, Kinsus, and others. CoWoS‑S is the density and signal‑integrity leader, but massive interposers require reticle stitching, carry high mask cost, face bow/warpage risks, and hit practical limits around 3.3× reticle unless yields are exceptionally high. (https://t.co/oi9tKsdRLQ, Applied Materials, Lam Research, HD Microsystems, Namics Corporation, Ajinomoto, Yahoo Finance)

How CoWoS‑R is built. CoWoS‑R deletes the giant silicon interposer and replaces it with an organic “RDL interposer” built up in polymer with multiple copper RDL layers. TSMC specifies 4 µm minimum pitch (2/2 µm L/S) and describes shielded ground‑signal stackups for high‑speed signaling. Because polymer has a lower modulus and different CTE, the RDL interposer acts as a mechanical buffer that reduces C4 bump strain energy density and improves reliability, and the RC of copper in polymer can be competitive at high frequencies. The tradeoff is lower routing density versus silicon and the inability to integrate on‑interposer eDTCs, which pushes more decoupling into the substrate or discrete components. CoWoS‑R improves cost and yield at large die sizes, which is why it appears on cost‑sensitive or moderately scaled parts like Trainium2. (https://t.co/oi9tKsdRLQ, TSMC Research, Semiconductor Engineering)

How CoWoS‑L is built. CoWoS‑L marries a wide‑pitch organic RDL interposer with embedded LSI “bridge” dice in the areas that need ultra‑dense die‑to‑die links. Those LSI islands bring sub‑micron copper lines and TSV access back into the structure and can also embed eDTC blocks under logic dies. The result is a reconstituted interposer that scales beyond 3.3× reticle, supports more HBM stacks with short high‑density links where needed, and improves cost/yield because the high‑value silicon is confined to small bridges rather than a dinner‑plate‑sized interposer. TSMC has said CoWoS‑L entered volume in 2024 and has since mapped a path to 5.5× and 9× reticle packages with 12 HBM stacks, which aligns with Blackwell’s migration to CoWoS‑L. Intel’s EMIB and Samsung’s I‑CubeE are broadly analogous “embedded bridge + organic RDL” approaches available outside TSMC. (https://t.co/oi9tKsdRLQ, TSMC, TrendForce, Intel, Samsung Semiconductor Global)

Manufacturers and who supplies what. Logic and bridges are overwhelmingly fabbed at TSMC for the chips on this roadmap, with Gaudi 3, NVIDIA Hopper/Blackwell, AMD MI3xx/MI350, Google TPU v6, and Microsoft Maia all using TSMC nodes. Packaging for those parts is TSMC 3DFabric CoWoS in Taiwan; TSMC is also localizing a small portion of advanced packaging with Amkor in Arizona for U.S. supply‑chain resiliency later in the decade. Samsung Foundry offers I‑Cube and X‑Cube as alternatives, and Intel Foundry Services offers EMIB and Foveros, which are strategically important where customers want non‑TSMC supply. HBM stacks come from SK hynix, Samsung, and Micron; SK hynix currently leads, Micron is guiding to 20‑25% share and has confirmed design‑ins on AMD MI350, and Samsung is expected to re‑accelerate with HBM4. ABF substrates and build‑up dielectrics center on Ajinomoto’s ABF material; substrate suppliers with exposure to AI accelerators include Ibiden, Shinko, Unimicron, AT&S, and Kinsus. Key equipment for CoWoS and HBM stacking includes copper ECD plating and wet cleans (Applied Materials, Lam), metrology/inspection (KLA, others), bonding/debonding and hybrid bonding for future HBM4/SoIC (EV Group, BESI), and underfill/encapsulants (Namics), along with polyimide/PBO dielectrics for RDL (HD Microsystems). (Intel CDRD, Amkor Technology, Samsung Semiconductor Global, Intel)

What this means brand by brand in 2025‑2027. For NVIDIA, CoWoS‑L is a risk and an opportunity. It is a necessary step to scale HBM count, package size, and bandwidth, but it introduces new yield and process‑integration variables versus the mature CoWoS‑S flow. Success depends on TSMC’s CoWoS‑L ramp and SK hynix/Micron/Samsung’s ability to supply HBM3E at 8‑high and 12‑high with acceptable thermals; tight CoWoS and HBM supply supports continued pricing power on Blackwell systems. For AMD, MI350 on CoWoS‑S should benefit from a stable process, larger HBM footprints, and Micron’s 12‑high HBM3E shipments; the main gating item is allocation of TSMC CoWoS and HBM supply. For Intel, Gaudi 3’s 128 GB HBM2E simplifies memory supply but risks losing on absolute bandwidth versus HBM3E/4 designs; it is priced to compete and leverages mature packaging. For Google and Microsoft, using CoWoS‑S with v6e and Maia 100 avoids the bleeding edge of CoWoS‑L and HBM3E qualification and has been explicitly framed as a TCO‑first design choice. For Amazon, Trainium2’s likely CoWoS‑R architecture suggests a deliberate cost/yield trade while still accessing HBM3E. For Meta, LPDDR5 keeps cost and power low for recommendation workloads while avoiding HBM entirely. The through‑line is that packaging choice is now a strategic lever for cost, yield, and time‑to‑ramp. (NVIDIA, Wccftech, Micron Technology, Intel CDRD, ServeTheHome, Amazon Web Services, Inc., Google Cloud)

The manufacturing playbook and where the bottlenecks live. In CoWoS‑S, the silicon interposer is processed with TSVs and multiple BEOL layers, HBM cubes are stacked by the memory vendors and delivered as known‑good stacks, then logic and HBM are micro‑bumped to the interposer with underfill and molding at wafer scale, followed by singulation and mount on ABF substrates. In CoWoS‑R, the interposer is reconstructed in polymer RDL on a carrier with multiple Cu layers and then assembled similarly. In CoWoS‑L, RDL build‑up proceeds, then LSI bridges are embedded in precise windows to deliver sub‑micron wiring only where needed, and eDTC blocks can be placed under logic dies to stabilize power delivery. The mechanical buffer properties of polymer and the lower RC of RDL at high frequency favor CoWoS‑R/L reliability, but organic RDL cannot match silicon interposer routing density; that is why bridges are necessary. Process control is non‑trivial for die warpage, coplanarity, and alignment in large packages; high‑throughput copper ECD, photosensitive polyimide RDL dielectrics, temporary wafer bonding/debonding, advanced underfill, and metrology are the scarce tools and materials. Those steps, not just the front‑end wafer fabs, are what gate shipments. (https://t.co/oi9tKsdRLQ, TSMC Research, Applied Materials, Lam Research, HD Microsystems, https://t.co/IprQfflBAf)

Investment implications for the portfolio. First, TSMC remains the single biggest beneficiary of AI accelerator growth because it captures value in both wafers and advanced packaging. The company more than doubled CoWoS capacity in 2024, is expanding again in 2025, and is raising CoWoS prices by 10‑20% as demand outstrips supply; its plan to scale to 5.5× and eventually 9× reticle packages reinforces a multi‑year packaging moat. The most straightforward expression is to overweight TSMC against cyclic noise in handsets/PCs, with the risk that any CoWoS‑L yield hiccup or geopolitical shock disrupts shipments. Second, HBM suppliers are structurally advantaged. SK hynix holds the technology lead and the largest NVIDIA wallet share; Micron has secured AMD MI350 with 12‑high HBM3E and targets 20‑25% market share by 2025; Samsung’s near‑term risk is credibility on HBM3E quality but HBM4 is a re‑set opportunity. A barbell of SK hynix for leadership plus Micron for share gains is justified; underweight Samsung near term if evidence of qualification delays persists, with optionality to add on HBM4 progress. Third, ABF substrate suppliers are leveraged to the “bigger package” trend. Ajinomoto’s ABF resin is the de facto standard, while Ibiden, Shinko, Unimicron, AT&S, and Kinsus are the substrate names with increasing high‑end mix; Ibiden is expanding capacity specifically for AI, and yield differentials versus peers matter. A basket approach can work given single‑name volatility and customer concentration. Fourth, OSAT and localized packaging are investable as de‑risking plays. Amkor’s Arizona plant agreement with TSMC creates a long‑dated U.S. advanced‑packaging option; the financial impact is back‑loaded but the strategic value is significant for domestic supply chains. Fifth, equipment and materials are secular winners. Applied Materials and Lam Research monetise copper ECD, cleans, and packaging‑class wet processing for RDL and Cu pillars; EV Group and BESI are leveraged to temporary bonding and the coming wave of hybrid bonding in HBM4 and SoIC; Namics benefits from molded/board underfills in HBM stacks; KLA benefits from metrology/inspection of advanced packages. These exposures carry lower headline risk than a single GPU vendor while capturing the capex flywheel. (TrendForce, Yahoo Finance, Amkor Technology, Applied Materials, Lam Research, https://t.co/IprQfflBAf)

Risk disclosures and what to monitor. CoWoS‑L yield and module reliability are the largest near‑term unknowns because they introduce new failure modes relative to CoWoS‑S; watch TSMC’s OIP and customer ramp commentary. HBM availability will stay tight through 2025; any stumble by a key supplier can materially constrain shipments. DRAM price volatility and policy risk (export controls, tariffs) can affect HBM procurement and margins; the pricing bias for DRAM and HBM into 2025 remains upward. Substrate yields and lead‑times are a tactical risk, especially for very large designs moving toward 5.5× reticle packages; substrate scaling and glass‑core initiatives could be a 2026‑2027 wildcard. Finally, packaging competition exists: Intel EMIB‑M/T and Samsung I‑CubeE provide non‑TSMC heterogenous integration options, and large CSPs could dual‑source packaging to diversify risk. We would size positions with these execution and policy risks in mind, and continuously re‑underwrite allocation as evidence accumulates that CoWoS‑L and HBM4 ramp on schedule. (TrendForce, Intel, Samsung Semiconductor Global)

Technical appendix on CoWoS types for committee review. CoWoS‑S is the canonical 2.5D flow: large silicon interposer with TSVs and fine BEOL, 3.3× reticle limit, on‑interposer eDTC, best‑in‑class density/latency/PDN, and highest cost and mask count. CoWoS‑R is an organic RDL interposer with 2/2 µm wiring and multiple Cu layers, better mechanical compliance and reliability at scale, but lower density and no interposer eDTC; think Trainium‑class parts or mid‑range HBM footprints. CoWoS‑L embeds small LSI bridges within an RDL interposer, regaining sub‑micron routing exactly where needed and enabling embedded eDTC under logic; it scales beyond 3.3× to 5.5× and 9× reticle, enabling 12 HBM stacks for 2026‑2027 designs. Intel’s EMIB family performs the same functional role as LSI bridges inside an advanced package, and Samsung’s I‑CubeE is its own “bridge + RDL” variant. This taxonomy explains why the chart shows NVIDIA shifting to CoWoS‑L at 192 GB HBM3E, AMD persisting on CoWoS‑S at 256‑288 GB, Google/Microsoft staying with CoWoS‑S for v6e/Maia 100, and Amazon opting for CoWoS‑R for Trainium2. (https://t.co/oi9tKsdRLQ, TrendForce, Intel, Samsung Semiconductor Global)

Concrete, high‑confidence facts the committee can anchor on: TSMC explicitly specifies CoWoS‑S to 3.3× reticle with eDTC, CoWoS‑R with 2/2 µm RDL and reliability benefits, and CoWoS‑L with embedded LSI and eDTC; it also states CoWoS‑L volume begins in 2024. NVIDIA confirms H200 at 141 GB HBM3E, and industry sources consistently report Blackwell at 192 GB with CoWoS‑L. AMD publicly positions MI325X/MI350 at 256‑288 GB with HBM3E and has Micron as an HBM3E supplier. Intel’s Gaudi 3 whitepaper confirms TSMC N5 and 128 GB HBM2E. Google states v6e doubles HBM capacity and bandwidth over v5e. TSMC’s CoWoS capacity expansion and pricing actions are corroborated by several trackers, and SK hynix/Micron/Samsung dynamics on HBM share and pricing are well covered by independent sources. These are the ground truths for position sizing. (https://t.co/oi9tKsdRLQ, TSMC, NVIDIA, Wccftech, AMD, Micron Technology, Intel CDRD, Google Cloud, TrendForce)

Bottom line for the portfolio: overweight the upstream bottlenecks (TSMC for CoWoS and wafers; SK hynix and Micron for HBM), add a measured basket of ABF substrate suppliers, and hold selective exposure to equipment and materials levered to advanced packaging and HBM. Underwrite NVIDIA, AMD, and the hyperscalers through the lens of packaging and HBM allocations rather than nominal die roadmaps; each has a credible path, but shipment curves will be determined by CoWoS lines, substrate availability, and HBM bins. The next structural catalysts are 5.5×/9× CoWoS‑L, HBM4 with hybrid bonding, and broader adoption of embedded‑bridge packaging across the industry; all 3 favor the capacity owners and the materials/equipment ecosystem that enables them. (TrendForce, https://t.co/xb6hj4oYpp)

Flash/NAND is now a first‑class resource in generative AI infrastructure rather than a passive repository. In the training path, datasets flow from object stores or shared filesystems into local NVMe tiers on the GPU hosts, then over GPUDirect Storage DMA paths straight into HBM; in the reverse direction, large periodic checkpoints are flushed back to flash before being drained to capacity tiers. NVIDIA’s own DGX storage reference architecture codifies this, calling for single‑node read bandwidth between 4–40 GB/s and write bandwidth between 2–20 GB/s depending on model type, and explicitly noting that checkpoint files can be “terabytes in size” and are synchronous blockers—hence the need for high‑throughput, low‑latency NVMe on each accelerator node. The same guidance recommends treating local NVMe as a cache or staging tier to avoid saturating the networked store, and pairs that with GPUDirect Storage so data moves directly between NVMe and GPU memory with minimal CPU overhead. This is the architectural reason flash rides alongside every modern AI GPU and why flash bandwidth and capacity scale with the number of accelerators deployed.  ￼

On NVIDIA’s rack‑scale platforms, the flash footprint is explicit and material. A GB200 NVL72 rack contains 18 compute trays; each tray integrates 2 Grace CPUs and 4 Blackwell GPUs and, crucially, 8 hot‑plug E1.S SSDs plus an M.2 boot device. HPE’s QuickSpecs list the baseline as 8×3.84 TB E1.S per tray, yielding 30.72 TB of node‑local NVMe. At full rack scale that is 18×30.72 TB = 552.96 TB of local flash before counting any disaggregated NVMe shelves in the same aisle. The same document shows 18 M.2 OS devices at 1.98 TB each, a non‑trivial but secondary contributor. In cloud form factors, Microsoft’s ND GB200 v6 advertises 4 local NVMe disks totaling 16 TB per host for the same purpose—fast data staging, scratch, and spill. On prior‑gen DGX H100 nodes, NVIDIA shipped 8×3.84 TB U.2 plus dual 1.92 TB M.2 OS devices, a configuration that has become a de facto minimum for 8‑GPU training boxes and a useful proxy for non‑NVLink systems. These platform‑level facts anchor flash content per GPU at roughly 7–16 TB depending on the node design and drive capacities selected.  ￼

AMD‑based AI servers follow the same storage physics. The Instinct MI350X carries 288 GB of HBM3E at 8 TB/s per GPU, so IO starvation is a real risk without robust NVMe tiers. Reference MI350X systems from OEMs show 8–12 front‑accessible U.2/U.3 bays per 8‑GPU chassis, with additional M.2 slots for OS or metadata. Configured with 15.36 TB TLC or QLC, that puts 122–184 TB of node‑local flash under a single 8‑GPU roof, most of which is used for local caching, preprocessed shard staging, and checkpoint buffering. Fundamentally, MI350X compute density raises the same storage requirement curve as GB200: per‑GPU flash capacity and bandwidth need to scale to keep accelerators fed and to ensure training resiliency.  ￼

Disaggregation adds a second engine of flash demand in AI “factories.” To keep accelerators busy across many nodes, hyperscalers deploy NVMe‑oF JBOFs and Ethernet‑attached “bunches of flash,” frequently fronted by DPUs. A typical JBOF with 24 U.2 or 36 E3.S bays turns into 1.5–2.2 PB of flash when populated with today’s 61.44 TB QLC drives, and can deliver 100+ GB/s per shelf with the right fabric and controller. Supermicro’s BlueField‑powered JBOF shows how the DPU terminates NVMe‑oF and acts as a PCIe root for the SSDs to minimize host CPU involvement, while GPUDirect Storage lets these shelves DMA straight into GPU memory at tens of GB/s per node. Meta’s RSC is the canonical at‑scale example: its storage system was architected for 16 TB/s and exabyte‑class capacity, with local and networked flash caches absorbing “first epoch” reads and accelerating non‑sequential access. As model sizes and dataset heterogeneity climb, this pooled NVMe layer grows faster than host‑local flash because it amortizes bandwidth across many accelerators and shortens time‑to‑first‑epoch.  ￼

Inference is becoming an equally important flash consumer. Two emerging patterns drive this: first, model weight staging for rapid cold starts and model swaps, especially with multi‑model serving, and second, tiered KV‑cache architectures that spill less‑recent attention keys/values to NVMe rather than DRAM or GPU memory. Open‑source stacks and vendors now describe disk‑resident KV caches that sharply raise hit rates on multi‑turn conversations; at cluster scale, systems like VAST’s VUA create global NVMe‑backed prefix caches that shrink time‑to‑first‑token, effectively “stretching” GPU memory with flash. The economic lever is straightforward: NVMe is far cheaper per GB than HBM or DDR5, so every percentage point of cache spilled to flash diverts budget to GPUs while raising utilization. That dynamic pushes significant flash attach into inference pods that may be far more numerous than training racks.  ￼

Drive technology is simultaneously removing capacity constraints and altering mix. Shipping enterprise NVMe spans from 7.68 TB TLC to 61.44 TB and 122.88 TB QLC today, with announced 122 TB E3.S and 245 TB E3.L on Micron’s 6600 ION roadmap and 122.88 TB already shown by Solidigm’s D5‑P5336. The shift to EDSFF E1.S/E3.S raises per‑node slots, power envelopes, and serviceability, which—combined with rising per‑drive capacities—pushes per‑rack flash into multi‑petabyte territory without explosive slot counts. Net effect: bit growth per AI rack accelerates even if the number of drives per node stays flat; with 18 compute trays, a baseline GB200 NVL72 already embeds ~0.55 PB of local flash using 3.84 TB E1.S, and the same chassis can scale its cache by simply slotting higher‑capacity media or adding a small number of JBOFs. This is a structurally different demand curve than classic CPU server refresh cycles.  ￼

Translating architecture into NAND bit demand: the scalar is “flash per accelerator.” With GB200 NVL72, the baseline works out to ~7.68 TB of NVMe per GPU from local E1.S alone; MI350X 8‑GPU boxes configured with 8×15.36 TB sit around 15.36 TB per GPU. Even assuming conservative adoption—say, 4–8 TB/GPU local plus 0.5–1.5 PB of pooled JBOF flash per rack—the math compounds fast. At 1,000 racks, that is roughly 0.5 EB of local NVMe plus 0.5–1.5 EB of pooled flash; at 10,000 racks, it is 5–20 EB, and that excludes downstream all‑flash arrays feeding pre‑processing, RAG indices, and vector databases attached to inference farms. Because these racks tend to be storage‑balanced at deployment and then upgraded in place as datasets and model catalogs grow, flash procurement is not a 1‑and‑done event; it repeats as more capacity is carved out for caching, new models, and higher QLC layer densities. The flow‑through to enterprise SSD revenue is already visible in quarterly data as Blackwell and other AI platforms ramp.  ￼

Pricing and supply are tightening around the enterprise SSD segment as AI growth collides with a still‑oligopolistic NAND industry. TrendForce has flagged enterprise SSD revenue up 12.7% QoQ in 2Q25 on AI server builds, and has also pointed to 3Q25 NAND contract price increases of 5–10% on low finished‑goods inventories; recent commentary additionally highlights periodic shortages in controller IC substrates and even DRAMs used as drive cache, which can pinch availability at the high‑capacity end. While the cyclical NAND industry can add die‑level supply with each node, high‑cap QLC drives depend on controller readiness, PCIe Gen5/Gen6 platform support, and the EDSFF supply chain, so enterprise SSD supply can be temporarily inelastic—exactly when hyperscalers want to lock in multi‑quarter volumes. The medium‑term counterweight is die density: Micron’s 122 TB E3.S and 245 TB E3.L designs and Solidigm’s 122.88 TB family suggest bit/drive will outpace rack slot growth from 2025–2027, which should gradually loosen capacity constraints even if attach per GPU keeps rising.  ￼

Workload mix determines TLC vs QLC demand. Training checkpoints and mixed read/write caches still lean TLC for endurance and QoS predictability, whereas dataset shards, prefix caches, and inference KV caches are mostly read‑dominant and increasingly land on QLC to minimize $/TB. Hyperscalers like Meta have publicly endorsed QLC as a strategic lever for data center economics, and vendors are pushing QLC‑first arrays and 60–122 TB NVMe for AI capacity tiers. That implies a sustained mix shift toward QLC at the rack and array level, with TLC concentrated in the per‑node write‑intensive tiers—exactly where the “hot path” performance and durability matter. Over time, controller‑level wear management and host‑managed placement are expanding QLC’s envelope even for lighter‑write checkpoint and pre‑processing tasks, increasing the proportion of AI‑driven NAND bits that are QLC.  ￼

The near‑term demand impulse is strongest at 2 layers of the stack: node‑local NVMe caches that scale roughly linearly with the accelerator base, and disaggregated NVMe pools that scale with cluster size and model catalog breadth. Inference multiplies the effect because there are more inference nodes than training nodes, and they increasingly rely on NVMe for low‑cost weight staging and KV‑cache tiers. With Blackwell and MI350X ramps, that is enough to swing the enterprise SSD market into periodic undersupply even if total NAND output across mobile and client remains ample. The macro wild cards are hyperscaler capex cadence and platform transitions; a broad slowdown in 2026 capex would temper growth, but the structural attach of flash to GPUs means the floor is higher than in prior cycles. On balance, the generative AI buildout should keep enterprise SSD demand growing faster than aggregate NAND supply through 2026, with pricing power accruing to high‑capacity QLC and to TLC SKUs aimed at write‑heavy training tiers, until 122–245 TB drives are pervasive and controller/EDSFF bottlenecks clear.

As of 2025, TSMC’s 3nm capacity is estimated to be around 100,000–120,000 wafer starts per month (WSPM), with plans to scale to 150,000 WSPM by 2026 as new facilities come online.
